config.title: Utility Types

intro.title: Utility Types
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React component that displays a user profile. You will learn how to use TypeScript's utility types, like `Partial` and `Pick`, to make your code more flexible and type-safe. The main technologies involved are React with TypeScript (TSX) and TypeScript's built-in utility types. By the end, you'll understand how to transform existing types to create new ones without rewriting code.
intro.usecase: Utility Types are essential in real-world React applications when you need to create flexible, reusable type definitions. For example, when building a dashboard with multiple filter panels, you might use `Partial<T>` to handle optional filter values or `Pick<T, K>` to extract only the properties needed for a specific chart component. In user management interfaces, `Omit<T, K>` helps create safe update forms by excluding read-only fields like user IDs. These types ensure type safety while reducing code duplication across complex applications with shared data structures.

objectives: Implement a utility type to create a new type from an existing interface.
Apply the Partial utility type to make all properties of an object optional.
Construct a type that omits specific properties using the Omit utility.
Configure a component to accept a subset of properties using the Pick utility.
Update a state object type to be read-only with the Readonly utility.
Manipulate union types to extract specific member types using the Extract utility.
Initialize a type that excludes certain union members with the Exclude utility.

steps.hint: Use import statements to bring in React and the utility types from 'react' and 'typescript' respectively.

steps.title: Define the base User interface
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface named 'User' with properties: id (number), name (string), email (string), and isActive (boolean).
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions with their types.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a User interface ready to use as a base type for utility type transformations later in the lesson.
successCriteria: A User interface is defined with the correct property names and types.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that all properties (id, name, email, isActive) are included with the correct types (number, string, string, boolean).
steps.feedbackWrong: The User interface is not correctly defined. Make sure to use the 'interface' keyword and define all four properties with their types.

steps.title: Initialize sample user data
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, create a constant named 'sampleUser' with the User interface type and assign it an object containing example user data.
steps.hint: Use the User interface you defined earlier to type the sampleUser object. Include properties like id, name, email, and isActive with appropriate values.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a typed sampleUser object ready to demonstrate utility type transformations in later steps.
successCriteria: sampleUser is typed with the User interface
sampleUser contains at least id, name, email, and isActive properties
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure sampleUser has all required properties from the User interface with correct types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The sampleUser object doesn't match the User interface requirements. Check that it includes id (number), name (string), email (string), and isActive (boolean).

steps.title: Create a Partial<User> type example
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create a variable named 'partialUserUpdate' with the type 'Partial<User>' and assign it an empty object.
steps.hint: Use the Partial utility type to make all properties of User optional. You can assign an empty object {} as the initial value.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a variable 'partialUserUpdate' with type 'Partial<User>' that can be used to represent partial user updates.
successCriteria: The 'partialUserUpdate' variable is declared with type 'Partial<User>' and initialized with an empty object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've declared 'partialUserUpdate' with the exact type 'Partial<User>' and assigned it an empty object {}.
steps.feedbackWrong: create a variable named 'partialUserUpdate' with type 'Partial<User>' inside the App component.

steps.title: Create a Required<User> type example
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create a new variable called 'completeUser' and type it as Required<User>. Initialize it with all properties from sampleUser plus an additional 'age' property set to 30.
steps.hint: Use the Required utility type to make all properties mandatory. The Required<User> type will require all properties from the User interface.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a 'completeUser' variable typed with Required<User> that demonstrates how the utility type makes all properties mandatory.
successCriteria: A variable named 'completeUser' is created with type Required<User> and contains id, name, email, and age properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the Required<User> type and including all required properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a variable called 'completeUser' with type Required<User> that includes id, name, email, and age properties.

steps.title: Create a Readonly<User> type example
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, create a variable named 'readonlyUser' with the type 'Readonly<User>' and assign it the value of 'sampleUser'.
steps.hint: Use the Readonly utility type to make all properties of the User interface immutable. The syntax is 'Readonly<User>'.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a 'readonlyUser' variable with type 'Readonly<User>' that contains the same data as 'sampleUser'.
successCriteria: The 'readonlyUser' variable is declared with type 'Readonly<User>' and assigned the value of 'sampleUser'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using the 'Readonly<User>' type annotation and assigning the 'sampleUser' value.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've created a variable named 'readonlyUser' with type 'Readonly<User>' and assigned it the 'sampleUser' value.

steps.title: Create a Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'> type example
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create a new constant named userContact with the type Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'> and assign it an object containing only the name and email properties from sampleUser.
steps.hint: Use the Pick utility type to select specific properties from the User interface. The syntax is Pick<Type, Keys> where Keys is a union of property names.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a userContact object with only name and email properties, typed using Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'>.
successCriteria: The userContact constant is declared with type Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'> and contains an object with name and email properties from sampleUser.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using the correct Pick syntax and including both name and email properties from sampleUser.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the syntax for Pick utility type. It should be Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'> and the object should contain only those two properties.

steps.title: Create an Omit<User, 'id' | 'isActive'> type example
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create a userProfile object using the Omit utility type to exclude the 'id' and 'isActive' properties from the User interface.
steps.hint: Use the Omit utility type to create a new type that excludes specific properties. Then declare a variable with that type and assign appropriate values.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a userProfile object that only contains name and email properties, demonstrating how Omit creates a type by excluding specified properties.
successCriteria: A userProfile object is declared using Omit<User, 'id' | 'isActive'> type with name and email properties assigned appropriate values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the Omit utility type correctly and excluding both 'id' and 'isActive' properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The userProfile object isn't created correctly. Remember to use Omit<User, 'id' | 'isActive'> to create a type that excludes those properties, then declare a variable with that type.

steps.title: Add the main container structure

steps.hint: Start by returning a <div> with a class name like 'container'. Inside, add an <h1> for the lesson title and separate sections for each utility type example you'll display later.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component returns a JSX structure with a container div, a main heading, and five sections with subheadings for each utility type.
successCriteria: The component returns a JSX structure containing a div with className 'container', an h1 with the lesson title, and five section elements each with an h2 for the utility type names.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have all the required elements: a container div, a main heading, and five sections with subheadings for each utility type.
steps.feedbackWrong: The structure doesn't match the expected JSX. Check that you're returning a container div with the correct heading and sections.

steps.title: Display the utility type examples in JSX
steps.instruction: Inside your component, create a variable named `partialUserUpdate` with type `Partial<User>` and assign it an object that updates only the email property.
steps.hint: Use the `Partial<User>` type to create an object that can have any subset of User properties. Initialize it with `{ email: 'newemail@example.com' }`.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a `partialUserUpdate` variable with the correct TypeScript type annotation that can be used to demonstrate partial updates.
successCriteria: The `partialUserUpdate` variable is declared with type `Partial<User>` and contains an object with at least the email property updated.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using the `Partial<User>` type annotation and providing an object with at least one property from the User interface.
steps.feedbackWrong: create a variable named `partialUserUpdate` with type `Partial<User>` and assign it an object that updates at least one property.

steps.instruction: Add a comment above each utility type variable declaration explaining what that utility type does.
steps.hint: Write a brief comment starting with // before each const declaration that uses a utility type.
steps.expectedOutcome: Each utility type variable declaration will have an explanatory comment above it.
successCriteria: Comments are added above each utility type variable declaration explaining what Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, and Omit do.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added some comments, but make sure each utility type variable has its own explanatory comment.
